Once numbering billions, industrial rail-era commercial hunting and hardwood deforestation collapsed flocks below sustainable breeding density; Martha died in 1914.
Brightly patterned arboreal gecko disappeared from Rodrigues in 1917 following widespread native forest loss and predation by introduced rats and cats.
North America's only native parrot vanished due to bottomland forest clearing, plumage hunting, and crop-pest eradication; Incas died in 1918.
Wild horse of the Eurasian steppes was hunted for meat, eradicated to protect pasture for domestic livestock, and absorbed by hybridization; the last captive died in 1918.
North African hartebeest subspecies was pushed into remote Atlas valleys by intensive trophy hunting and French colonial campaigns, dying out in the 1920s.
Once-abundant freshwater fish collapsed rapidly after bush clearance warmed shaded streams and introduced brown and rainbow trout outcompeted and preyed on it.
Both Norfolk and Lord Howe subspecies perished by 1923 after introduced black rats raided nests, European starlings competed for hollows, and settlers shot them.
Iconic golden-state bear was systematically trapped, poisoned, and shot by Gold Rush settlers and ranchers protecting cattle, with the last seen in 1924.
Decimated by deforestation, Russian Civil War poaching, and cattle diseases like foot-and-mouth, the last wild Caucasian bison was shot on Mount Alous in 1927.
Termite-mound nesting Australian parrot perished from severe drought, overgrazing of seed grasses, trapping for aviculture, and feral cat predation.
Smallest equid subspecies was devastated by First World War military hunting, motorized pursuit, and grazing competition; the last died at Schönbrunn Zoo in 1927.
Restricted to a tiny offshore islet after mongooses overran mainland Guadeloupe, its final refuge was obliterated by the catastrophic 1928 Okeechobee hurricane.
Tiny forest insectivore disappeared within a decade of the 1918 SS Makambo shipwreck that unleashed black rats across Lord Howe Island.
Known from a single specimen taken below Jackson Lake Dam, this endemic sucker disappeared after dam construction altered flows and blocked spawning runs.
Bottom-dwelling sculpin vanished in the 1930s when severe drought and irrigation withdrawals shrank Utah Lake while salinity and introduced carp surged.
Coconut-defoliating Fijian moth became a rare intentional extinction target after entomologists introduced a parasitic tachinid fly for biological control.
Host-specific moth whose caterpillars fed on American chestnut bark suffered co-extinction after introduced chestnut blight fungus wiped out mature host trees.
Endemic Santa Cruz rice rat vanished within years of invasive black rats colonizing the island, bringing competition and introduced pathogens.
Tiny bark-mining moth vanished in a classic co-extinction cascade after the Asian chestnut blight decimated American chestnut forests across eastern North America.
Unique silver-blue char native to only two New Hampshire ponds was wiped out by overfishing and predation from introduced warm-water fish and trout.
Mollusk-crushing desert minnow restricted to springs near Parras de la Fuente perished when agricultural pumping drained its spring habitats and polluted waters.
Burrowing desert bandicoot vanished from central Australia due to fierce predation by introduced red foxes and feral cats alongside rabbit-driven habitat degradation.
Large flightless carabid beetle endemic to tiny Stephens Island was lost after forest clearing and introduced predators destroyed its coastal forest refuge.
Once abundant along Atlantic coastal barrens, overhunting reduced it to Martha’s Vineyard, where wildfires, severe winters, goshawks, and poultry disease killed the last male in 1932.
Known to science from a single 1932 skull, this spinifex-dwelling desert wallaby succumbed to feral cats, red foxes, and altered Indigenous fire regimes.
Builder of massive communal twig mounds across arid Australia was wiped out by introduced sheep grazing, rabbits, feral cats, and red foxes.
Prized for golden underwing tufts used in Hawaiian featherwork, it succumbed to habitat loss, introduced black rats, and mosquito-borne avian malaria.
Native rice rat of Santa Cruz and Baltra islands disappeared by 1934 after invasive black rats colonized the islands and spread disease.
Thought extinct until rediscovered in 1931 in the Lake Eyre basin, this hardy arid-zone marsupial vanished after 1935 under fox and cat predation and cattle grazing.
Subtropical laurel-forest pigeon of Okinawa and the Daitō Islands disappeared after military and agricultural deforestation and hunting.
Largest carnivorous marsupial hunted under government bounties to protect sheep flocks, compounded by habitat loss and disease; Benjamin died at Hobart Zoo.
Endemic sand-dune katydid known from a single 1937 specimen was only formally named after industrial sand mining and housing destroyed its Antioch Dunes habitat.
Smallest tiger population was restricted to tiny Bali and wiped out by Dutch colonial sport hunting, native prey loss, and clearing of monsoon forests.
Basket-antlered swamp deer lost its flood-plain habitat across Thailand’s Chao Phraya basin to commercial rice farming and was hunted out by 1938.
Endemic to the Rhine River between Mainz and Cologne, it vanished after severe industrial chemical pollution and riverbank engineering rendered the river uninhabitable.
Graceful, brightly striped Australian wallaby was hunted relentlessly for pelts and sport with greyhounds while swamps were drained and foxes invaded.
Large herbivorous skink restricted to Branco and Raso islets perished after prolonged droughts, human harvesting for food and oil, and introduced cats and rats.
Spring-fed desert minnow disappeared by 1940 as rapid groundwater pumping and urban development dried up Las Vegas Springs.
First North American butterfly driven extinct by urban development; coastal sand-dune construction in San Francisco eradicated its deerweed host plants.
Desert oasis amphibian was last collected in 1942 before groundwater extraction dried spring marshes and introduced American bullfrogs preyed on survivors.
Arid-zone marsupial vanished after 1943 due to predation from feral cats and red foxes compounded by rabbit competition and altered fire patterns.
Clear-cutting of vast old-growth bottomland hardwood swamps across the American South and Cuba alongside specimen hunting extinguished its last confirmed US populations by 1944.
Introduced rabbits denuded Laysan Island of vegetation, and a translocated refuge colony on Midway Atoll was wiped out when rats escaped wartime ships in 1944.
Blind subterranean aquatic diving beetle endemic to a single karst aquifer in southern France vanished due to groundwater pollution and extraction.
Only native land bird of Wake Atoll was hunted to complete extinction for food by starving stranded Japanese garrison troops during World War II blockade.
Warm-spring desert poolfish disappeared soon after 1948 due to spring modifications and predation from introduced crayfish, mosquitofish, and bullfrogs.
Lake Geneva deepwater whitefish succumbed to severe commercial overfishing and mid-century agricultural eutrophication that suffocated spawning beds.
Stilt-legged arid marsupial collapsed across Australia under feral cat and red fox predation combined with livestock trampling and altered fire regimes.
Montane Yemeni gazelle has not been reliably recorded since five specimens were collected near Taʻizz in 1951, wiped out by unregulated rifle hunting.
Unwary tropical seal was slaughtered for lamp oil and meat since Columbus’s voyages and starved by overfishing of reef prey; the last colony was seen at Serranilla Bank in 1952.
Largest Great Lakes cisco collapsed from intensive gillnet commercial fishing paired with devastating predation by invasive sea lampreys.
Confined to a single tiny Honduran coral island, this guinea-pig-like rodent was wiped out by Hurricane Janet in 1955 after feral house cats ravaged its population.
Tame melodious forest passerine declined drastically following North Island deforestation and predation by introduced ship rats and stoats.
Eastern Australian native rodent disappeared after agricultural land clearing fragmented woodlands and feral cats and foxes proliferated.
Small desert wallaby vanished from Western and central Australia due to red fox and feral cat predation combined with pastoral grazing.
World’s largest woodpecker perished after clear-cutting eradicated old-growth Durango pine forests in Mexico’s Sierra Madre Occidental and hunters shot survivors.
Diminutive Ohio riffle catfish known from a single Big Darby Creek site has not been seen since 1957, lost to agricultural runoff and siltation.
Formerly abundant California Central Valley marsh minnow disappeared after 95% of floodplain wetlands were drained for agriculture and invasive bass arrived.
North Africa’s iconic dark-maned lion population was hunted out of the Maghreb with modern firearms and state bounties, disappearing from the wild by the 1960s.
Harmless endemic Barbadian snake was driven to extinction by agricultural habitat loss and intense predation from the introduced small Indian mongoose.
Once numbering in the millions, relentless 19th-century market gunning on prairies and pampas alongside Rocky Mountain locust extinction collapsed its flocks by 1963.
Scarlet-and-orange Hawaiian honeycreeper persisted in remote Molokaʻi cloud forests until 1963 before mosquito-borne avian malaria and forest degradation ended it.
Forest songbird of New Zealand’s South Island plummeted in the late 19th century as introduced stoats, ship rats, and cats decimated ground-foraging birds.
Last grizzly population south of the US border was poisoned with Compound 1080 and trapped out by ranchers across Chihuahua’s Sierra del Nido.
Refugial shorebird survived on Big South Cape Island until a 1964 ship-rat invasion wiped out the last individuals despite desperate rescue attempts.
region: Stewart & Big South Cape Islands, New Zealand

cause: Valuable commercial fish of Lakes Erie and Ontario collapsed in the 1960s from heavy overfishing, industrial eutrophication, and invasive rainbow smelt.
Spring-dwelling livebearer vanished from the wild around Monterrey due to urban water extraction, sewage pollution, and introduced invasive fish.
World’s largest earwig (8 cm) vanished from Saint Helena’s Horse Point Plain due to surface rock removal for construction and predation by invasive mice and centipedes.
Flightless nocturnal carabid endemic to Saint Helena has not been seen since 1967 following dryland degradation and predation from introduced rodents and mynas.
Small endemic fruit bat was driven extinct on Guam by traditional culinary hunting, habitat clearing, and rampant predation by the introduced brown tree snake.
Deepwater salmonid of the upper Great Lakes vanished by 1969 under intense commercial trawling and invasive sea lamprey parasitism.
Extraordinarily long-billed Hawaiian honeycreeper succumbed to hurricane destruction of Alakaʻi forest habitat and deadly avian malaria and pox.
Extirpated across Central Asia by Soviet tugai river-forest reclamation for cotton irrigation, prey depletion, and state predator bounties.
Endemic California lake minnow died out around 1970 after tributary spawning streams were diverted for irrigation and introduced silversides and bluegill outcompeted fry.
Desert gazelle was wiped out across the Arabian Peninsula by motorized hunting parties; putative captive herds proved to be hybrids or different species.
Desert pupfish restricted to Monkey Spring in Arizona went extinct after groundwater overdraft shrank springs and non-native largemouth bass were introduced.
Nearly flightless New Zealand acanthisittid wren was driven off all three main islands by stoats and cats before a 1964 ship-rat invasion wiped out its final islet refuges.
Known from a single skull found in 1972, this island microbat perished due to predation by introduced owls and black rats after the 1918 shipwreck.
Island ground-foraging dove vanished from Socorro Island after 1972 due to feral cat predation and severe understory destruction by introduced sheep; kept alive in aviaries.
Mass commercial harvesting for leather, oil, and circus capture along with wartime naval disturbance and overfishing eradicated breeding rookeries by the 1970s.
Endemic Levantine cyprinid went extinct after the 1950s drainage of Lake Hula marshes for agriculture eliminated its spawning habitat.
Deepwater alpine lake whitefish perished when mid-century phosphorus pollution caused eutrophication and depleted deep oxygen needed for egg incubation.
Great Lakes deepwater whitefish was last caught in 1975 after decades of heavy gillnet fishing and parasitic predation by invasive sea lampreys.
Mainstem Rio Grande minnow vanished after major dams blocked flows, agricultural irrigation dewatered reaches, and pollution degraded river habitat.
Unique split-jawed snake survived only on Round Island off Mauritius until introduced goats and rabbits stripped soil-holding palm forests, causing habitat collapse by 1975.
Bright yellow Mexican goodeid disappeared from the wild Río Teuchitlán due to severe water diversion, agrochemical runoff, and invasive tilapia; maintained in aquaria.
Dense human expansion cleared Java’s lowland forests and depleted Rusa deer prey, while relentless poisoning and hunting wiped out the last Meru Betiri tigers in the 1970s.
Highland Andean wetland grebe vanished by 1977 following wetland drainage, pesticide runoff, reed harvesting, and predation of chicks by introduced rainbow trout.
Distinctive island butterfly endemic to Madeira’s laurel forests declined precipitously after small white butterfly introduction and agricultural pesticide use, last seen in 1977.
Overtrapped for export pelts and poisoned by post-war industrial river pollution and concrete bank canalization; the last verified individual was seen in Kōchi in 1979.
Heat-tolerant Mojave hot-spring fish became the first US Endangered Species Act animal declared extinct after bathhouse channelization fused outflows and triggered hybridization.
Endemic to Kunming’s Lake Dian, this colorful salamander was wiped out after 1979 by severe urban sewage pollution, lakeside reclamation, and introduced predatory carp.
Hybrid-origin island duck succumbed to wetland drainage for agriculture, World War II habitat destruction, and illegal hunting; the last captive died in 1981.
Discovered only in 1967 on a single 10-hectare strip of Aldabra Atoll, it was wiped out by introduced black rats, feral cats, and feral goats by 1983.
Endemic monarch flycatcher plummeted along with Guam’s native avifauna after the accidentally introduced brown tree snake swept across the island’s forests.
Restricted to a short stretch of the spring-fed San Marcos River, it succumbed to groundwater depletion, urban runoff, invasive plants, and hybridization with western mosquitofish.
Remarkable frog that incubated tadpoles in its stomach vanished within a decade of discovery due to chytridiomycosis fungal outbreaks and timber-harvest siltation.
Short-winged endemic grebe of Madagascar’s Lake Alaotra disappeared due to drowning in nylon gillnets, predatory invasive snakehead fish, and hybridization.
Discovered in Eungella rainforest streams in 1984 and extinct in the wild just a year later, felled by an explosive epidemic of lethal chytrid fungus.
Submergence of Goodenough Spring beneath Amistad Reservoir in 1968 eradicated its wild habitat, and captive hatchery stocks perished through mosquitofish hybridization by 1987.
Cordgrass marsh flooding for Cape Canaveral mosquito control, DDT spraying, and highway draining collapsed its range; the last individual died at Discovery Island in 1987.
region: Merritt Island & St. Johns River, Florida, USA

cause: Last member of the entire Hawaiian honeyeater family Mohoidae perished from invasive rats, habitat-degrading hurricanes, and avian malaria; its final mating call was recorded in 1987.
Atlantic Forest cracid was hunted out and lost nearly all habitat to Brazilian sugarcane plantations by 1988, surviving today solely through captive-bred descendants.
Canebrake-nesting migratory songbird perished from wholesale clearing of southern US floodplain bamboo swamps and Cuban wintering forests.
Predation by the invasive brown tree snake extirpated all wild birds on Guam by 1988; 29 captured survivors founded an ongoing captive breeding population.
Flightless giant grebe of Lake Atitlán collapsed after introduced largemouth bass devoured chicks, shoreline reeds were cut, and a 1976 earthquake dropped lake levels.
Monteverde cloud-forest endemic vanished rapidly after severe El Niño drying and lethal chytridiomycosis fungal outbreaks.
Parrot-billed Hawaiian honeycreeper once common across six islands collapsed due to mosquito-borne avian malaria, feral pig habitat damage, and invasive rats.
Large Kauaʻi thrush succumbed to avian malaria spread by introduced mosquitoes, black rat predation, and severe hurricane devastation of montane rainforests.
Upland Australian stream-breeding treefrog disappeared abruptly in 1990 following chytridiomycosis epidemics sweeping through Wet Tropics rainforests.
Laramie Basin glacial-relict toad collapsed from chytrid fungus, mosquito pesticides, and irrigation changes, leaving it Extinct in the Wild outside managed enclosures since 1991.
Bright crimson cloud-forest poison frog vanished from western Panama after 1992 under relentless deforestation, pet-trade collection, and chytrid fungus.
Endemic to a single spring pond at El Potosí in Nuevo León, its habitat dried up from agricultural groundwater extraction and invasive bass introduction by 1994.
Montane stream toad of Costa Rica and Panama suffered total population collapse by 1996 when chytridiomycosis swept through Talamancan cloud forests.
Curved-bill insectivorous Maui honeycreeper succumbed to highland forest degradation by feral pigs and upward expansion of malaria-carrying mosquitoes.
Once-abundant torrent frog of north Queensland collapsed precipitously across 1988–1997 under devastating outbreaks of amphibian chytridiomycosis.
Hunted for centuries and outcompeted by domestic livestock; last wild individual Celia died in 2000, followed by a brief 2003 cloning attempt.
Caraibeira gallery-forest clearing, Africanized honeybee hive competition, and relentless illegal wildlife trafficking wiped out the last wild bird in Bahia in 2000.
Intelligent ʻalalā corvid disappeared from wild Hawaiʻi forests in 2002 after habitat degradation, toxoplasmosis from feral cats, ʻio hawk predation, and avian malaria.
Masked Maui honeycreeper discovered only in 1973 declined due to invasive feral pigs, rats, and avian malaria; the last known bird died in captivity in 2004.
Declared functionally extinct in 2006 due to rolling-hook fishing gear, vessel strikes, Three Gorges damming, and severe river pollution.
First mammal extinction attributed directly to anthropogenic climate change; rising sea levels and storm-surge inundation destroyed vegetation on its low Torres Strait coral cay.
Tiny endemic bat collapsed from predation by introduced yellow crazy ants, wolf snakes, and giant centipedes; its final echolocation call faded into silence in August 2009.
Live-bearing gorge waterfall toad lost 90% of its mist habitat to a 2000 hydroelectric dam before chytrid fungus wiped out the remaining wild population by 2009.
Formerly abundant iridescent skink was driven extinct in the wild by 2010 primarily by predation from the accidentally introduced common wolf snake.
Atlantic Forest ovenbird restricted to tiny forest fragments amid northeastern Brazilian sugarcane estates was last seen in 2011 and declared extinct by BirdLife.
Relentless illegal poaching for traditional horn trade and habitat fragmentation decimated savanna populations in Cameroon until the IUCN declared it extinct in 2011.
Endemic Christmas Island gecko vanished from wild forests by 2012 due to predation by invasive wolf snakes, giant centipedes, and yellow crazy ants.
Whaler harvesting and invasive feral goats stripped Pinta Island vegetation; Lonesome George, the last pure individual, died in 2012.
Endemic Taiwanese felid population suffered relentless pelt trapping, lowland forest logging, and prey loss; declared extinct in 2013 after 15-year camera-trap surveys found none.
Diminutive spring pupfish lost its sole natural spring to groundwater pumping in 1994, and the final aquarium survivors perished in 2014.
Driven out of wild forests by invasive wolf snakes, giant centipedes, and crazy ants, the last known individual named Gump died in captivity in May 2014.
Gliding Panamanian canopy frog collapsed when chytridiomycosis struck El Valle de Antón; Toughie, the final known individual, died in Atlanta in 2016.
Overfishing and the 1981 Gezhouba Dam blocking upstream spawning migrations doomed this ancient 7-meter freshwater giant.
Known from a single 1862 Jakarta fish-market specimen, it was declared extinct by the IUCN in December 2023—the first marine fish lost to intensive coastal fishing and habitat degradation.
Migratory Eurasian shorebird not reliably seen since 1995 was formally declared extinct in late 2024 after wetland drainage along its Mediterranean flyway and hunting collapsed its population.
Spiral-horned Sahara desert antelope pushed under 100 wild individuals in Niger and Chad by motorized armed poaching, oil exploration disturbance, and severe regional droughts.
Recognized as a distinct species in 2021 and assessed as Critically Endangered after declining >86% over 31 years due to organized ivory poaching and slow reproduction.
Uplisted to Critically Endangered in 2024 after plunging below ~10,000 breeding pairs due to commercial purse-seine overfishing and climate-driven eastward shifts of sardine and anchovy stocks.
Largest terrestrial animal declined >60% over 50 years from industrial ivory poaching and shrinking migratory savanna corridors amidst human-agricultural expansion.
Wild ancestor of the domestic donkey reduced to <200 mature individuals in Eritrea and Ethiopia due to hunting for meat and medicine, livestock water competition, and interbreeding.
Wide-ranging pack predator (~6,600 individuals remaining) severely affected by habitat fragmentation, wire snares, roadkill, human-livestock conflict, and domestic-dog viral outbreaks.

Previously assessed as Near Threatened under heavy high-seas driftnet and longline pressure, high-seas driftnet bans alongside enforceable regional catch quotas by tuna RFMOs rebuilt global stocks enough to earn IUCN downlisting to Least Concern in 2021.

Driven down to fewer than 800 geese by arctic foxes introduced for fur farming across Aleutian nesting islands, systematic fox eradications, hunting closures, and winter pasture protection boosted the population above 100,000 and secured U.S. ESA delisting in 2001.

Hunted nearly to extinction until fewer than 100 individuals survived in Italy’s Gran Paradiso royal hunting reserve in the 1850s, royal protection, national park status, and cross-border Alpine reintroductions rebuilt wild populations above 50,000 animals.

Plummeted due to unregulated hide hunting and wetland drainage before gaining federal endangered status in 1967, strict poaching bans, CITES trade controls, and wetland protection sparked a dramatic comeback past 3 million animals and full U.S. ESA delisting in 1987.

Reduced across much of the eastern and lower U.S. by 1900 due to forest clearing and unregulated shooting, hardwood forest regrowth, state wildlife management, and the recovery and 2016 U.S. ESA delisting of the Louisiana black bear rebuilt continental numbers above 800,000.
region: North America (United States, Canada & Northern Mexico)

cause: Lost from >90% of its historic eastern North American range following prairie conversion, artificial night lighting, and the extinction/collapse of carrion-sized birds like the passenger pigeon.
Breeds exclusively on a tiny bog plateau on Amsterdam Island (~50–60 breeding pairs), vulnerable to avian cholera, feral cat/rat predation, and Southern Ocean pelagic longline bycatch.
Threatened by severe habitat fragmentation, wild prey scarcity, and illegal poaching (~120 wild individuals remaining in Primorsky Krai & NE China).
High-altitude (~3,000–5,000 m) wild felid numbering <1,400 mature individuals, imperiled by mountain chinchilla prey loss, lithium and copper mining, and traditional ceremonial hunting.
Bottom-dwelling European ambush shark extirpated from the North Sea and most of the Mediterranean by demersal trawling; its last major stronghold is the Canary Islands.
Smallest leopard subspecies (<120 wild individuals remaining in Oman and Yemen), driven to near-collapse by pastoralist retaliatory poisoning, ibex prey depletion, and mountain habitat loss.
Extinct in the Wild by 1972 due to motorized hunting; Operation Oryx captive breeding restored >1,000 wild individuals across Arabian reserves.

Fragmented into disconnected pockets across 13 Asian countries (~40,000–50,000 individuals) by rail/road corridors, agriculture, fatal electrocutions, and ivory/skin poaching; its Sumatran subspecies is CR.
Once ranged from Arabia to India; fewer than 30 individuals survive solely in central Iran's arid plains, killed by highway traffic, shepherd dogs, livestock conflict, and gazelle depletion.

Overfished toward commercial collapse across the Atlantic and Mediterranean by the 2000s, strict ICCAT recovery quotas, minimum-size rules, and electronic catch documentation allowed spawning biomass to surge and prompted an IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Least Concern in 2021.

Driven to Critically Endangered status by spearfishers and commercial targeting of spawning aggregations, a complete U.S. harvest moratorium enacted in 1990 together with mangrove nursery protection drove strong Florida rebounds and IUCN downlisting to Vulnerable in 2018.
Fewer than 1,500 mature individuals persist along West African nearshore waters, heavily depleted by coastal gillnet entanglement and direct bushmeat hunting.
Slow-breeding endemic whose colonies declined >60% over three generations due to historical sealing, gillnet drowning, marine debris entanglement, and hookworm disease.
Wild Lake Xochimilco population plummeted due to Mexico City urbanization, water pollution, and invasive carp and tilapia predation.
World's largest nocturnal primate suffers severe deforestation of Malagasy rainforests plus targeted persecution in areas where local folklore treats it as a bad omen.

Confined to degraded mountain fragments with fewer than 100 pairs when invasive Himalayan ginger and Japanese cedar overtook native laurel forest, EU LIFE habitat-restoration projects cleared invasives and replanted native flora, lifting numbers past 1,000 and earning downlisting to Vulnerable in 2016.
Central America's largest native land mammal (<4,500 individuals), squeezed by rapid cattle-pasture deforestation, highway roadkill, and illegal subsistence hunting.
Recovered from 417 nesting pairs in 1963 to >71,000 pairs today after banning DDT pesticides, protecting nesting wetlands, and enforcing federal protections.
Snow-white songbird driven down to just ~6 wild birds in 2001 by rampant trapping for Indonesia's cage-bird trade; ongoing releases maintain small wild flocks under constant poaching pressure.
Uplisted to Critically Endangered in 2024 as wild herds across mainland Southeast Asia, Java, and Borneo plummeted (>80% decline in Cambodia) from snaring, meat poaching, and hybridization.
Second-largest fish remains severely depleted from historic liver-oil harpooning and ongoing trawl entanglement, slow reproductive maturity, and surface vessel collisions.

Extirpated from the European Alps by 1913 due to myths that it preyed on livestock, an international captive-breeding and release partnership begun in 1986 re-established self-sustaining wild breeding pairs across the Alpine arc.
region: European Alps, Pyrenees, Caucasus & Asian Highlands

cause: World's largest freshwater-spawning fish (up to 7 m) pushed to the brink by relentless poaching for luxury black caviar and Soviet-era dams blocking >90% of Volga and Danube spawning beds.

Reduced to fewer than 20,000 animals by 1900 from overhunting and pneumonia transmitted by domestic sheep, mountain wildlife refuges, separation from domestic flocks, and hundreds of helicopter trap-and-transfer reintroductions rebuilt herds above 70,000.
region: Rocky Mountains & Southwestern Deserts, North America

cause: Intertidal rocky-shore snail decimated >90% by historical commercial harvest and fatal withering syndrome (bacterial infection exacerbated by El Niño and warming coastal waters).

Hunted close to commercial extinction across the Amazon by the 1970s for its prized ventral hide, CITES trade prohibitions, protected várzea floodplain reserves like Mamirauá, and Indigenous community management drove strong rebounds across Brazil, Ecuador, and French Guiana.
Lost 96% of its numbers in the late 20th century to horn poaching; despite gradual recovery past ~6,400 animals under armed protection, illegal syndicate poaching remains acute.
World's rarest wading bird (~160–200 wild adults in New Zealand's Mackenzie Basin), decimated by braided-river hydropower alteration and introduced stoats, ferrets, and feral cats.
region: Mackenzie Basin, South Island, New Zealand

cause: Brought to the brink of total extinction around 1900 with fewer than 600 animals surviving on two South African farms, farmer stewardship, provincial nature reserves, and nationwide restocking onto wildlife ranches rebuilt numbers above 18,000.
Canopy-dwelling seed disperser projected to decline >80% over three generations from slash-and-burn tavy farming, selective logging, and targeted hunting.

Previously assessed as Endangered and Vulnerable due to severe longline and trawl bycatch mortality, mandatory bird-scaring streamer lines, weighted hooks, and night-setting rules across Southern Ocean fisheries halted declines and drove IUCN downlisting to Least Concern in 2017.

Listed as U.S. Endangered in 1987 with fewer than 350 known individuals, brushland habitat management on military lands, ranches, and refuges alongside cowbird control restored more than 14,000 singing males and achieved full ESA delisting in 2018.
Thought extinct until 18 ferrets were rediscovered in Wyoming in 1981; captive propagation and prairie-dog habitat protection restored wild colonies.
Earth's largest animal remains at a fraction of pre-whaling abundance (~10,000–25,000 individuals), pressured by ship strikes, ocean noise, entanglement, and krill-stock warming.
Endemic to Bolivia's Beni savannas (~350–450 wild birds), driven to rarity by historical pet trapping and cattle-ranch burning of motacú palm groves needed for nesting cavities.
Restricted south of the Congo River in the DRC, threatened by commercial bushmeat poaching fueled by civil instability, expanding logging roads, and human-borne disease.
region: Congo Basin (South of Congo River), DRC

cause: Threatened as U.S. Endangered in 1982 by geothermal drilling and water diversion at its sole 10-acre thermal lake, Nature Conservancy land acquisition, vehicle fencing, and the Steens Mountain geothermal withdrawal protected the aquifer and earned ESA delisting in 2020.
One of the world's least-known wild cats, strictly endemic to Borneo (~2,200 mature individuals) and declining rapidly alongside lowland dipterocarp logging and agricultural conversion.
Lost >100,000 individuals in two decades to lowland rainforest conversion for oil palm and timber, exacerbated by El Niño peatland fires and retaliatory killing.

Nearly wiped out across Arctic basins by commercial whaling through 1915, international commercial bans and co-managed Indigenous subsistence quotas allowed the Bering–Chukchi–Beaufort and eastern Canadian stocks to rebound above 16,000 whales and achieve IUCN Least Concern status.
Shark-like ray prized for its massive fins (among the highest-priced in shark-fin markets) and flattened across Indo-Pacific shelves by heavy bottom-trawl and gillnet fishing.

Wiped out across most of Western Europe and the contiguous U.S. outside Yellowstone and Glacier parks, strict hunting limits, European Habitats Directive corridor protection, and Yellowstone grizzly recovery increased populations across Scandinavia, the Alps, and the Northern Rockies.
region: Europe, Northern Asia & Northwestern North America

cause: Extirpated as a breeder in Louisiana and imperiled across North America by DDT and endrin pesticide pollution, the 1972 U.S. DDT ban and coastal colony restoration rebuilt populations past 650,000 birds, leading to full U.S. Endangered Species Act delisting in 2009.

Endangered after wetland drainage and predation by stoats and feral cats, captive breeding releases coupled with coordinated community predator control along coastal streams rebuilt populations and earned IUCN downlisting to Near Threatened.
region: Northland, Great Barrier Island & Sanctuaries, New Zealand

cause: Brought back from 27 total birds in 1987 through bold captive breeding, lead-ammunition bans, and intensive reintroduction to >560 birds.

Exterminated on main Campbell Island by Norway rats and restricted to tiny Dent Island with roughly 50 survivors, captive breeding and the world’s largest rat-eradication campaign in 2001 allowed successful reintroduction back onto Campbell Island and IUCN downlisting to Vulnerable in 2020.
region: Campbell & Dent Islands, Subantarctic New Zealand

cause: Rediscovered in 2002 after decades presumed extinct; ~75–135 individuals survive in karst limestone forest along the Vietnam–China border amid firewood gathering and grazing.

Reduced to fewer than 80 individuals across fragmented mountain farms in the 1930s, creation of Mountain Zebra National Park in 1937 and coordinated private and state reserve translocations multiplied the subspecies above 5,000 and secured IUCN downlisting to Least Concern in 2019.
Only marine mammal of the landlocked Caspian Sea; plummeted from ~1 million a century ago due to ice-sheet warming, sturgeon-poaching net drowning, and toxic pollution.

By 1980 only five individuals survived, including a single fertile female named "Old Blue"; Don Merton’s cross-fostering program using Chatham Island tomtits and predator-free island restoration multiplied the population past 250 adults, earning IUCN downlisting to Vulnerable in 2022.
Humanity's closest living relative faces widespread deforestation, commercial bushmeat hunting, wire-snare maiming, and Ebola/respiratory outbreaks; the Western subspecies is Critically Endangered.
Only Old World alligator survives with ~150–300 wild individuals in tiny agricultural wetland fragments of Anhui Province, threatened by habitat loss, agrochemicals, and snail-bait poisoning.
World's largest amphibian (up to 1.8 m) wiped from almost all wild mountain streams by luxury-food poaching, damming, river siltation, and genetic swamping from escaped farmed hybrids.
Decimated across southern China and the Himalayan foothills by massive illegal poaching for meat and keratin scales prized in traditional medicine, alongside slow single-offspring breeding.

Eliminated across large portions of Western Europe by poisoned baits and habitat loss, strict anti-poisoning enforcement, vulture feeding stations ("muladares"), and reintroductions in France, Portugal, and the Balkans have rebuilt European colonies.

Extinct as a British breeder for roughly four centuries and severely reduced across Western Europe by hunting and fen drainage, peatland protection, agri-environment winter feeding, and Britain’s Great Crane Project reintroduction spurred broad population growth.

Once declining steeply from feral cats, kiore rats, and weka on offshore breeding islands, complete mammalian predator eradications on Hauturu (Little Barrier Island) and Whenua Hou (Codfish Island) reversed nest losses and earned IUCN downlisting to Vulnerable in 2008.
Restricted to a tiny remnant (<5%) of Colombia's tropical dry forest after massive cattle-ranching clearance and historic export of tens of thousands for biomedical research and pet trade.

Eliminated across eastern North America and reduced to roughly 20–30 inbred Florida panthers in the 1970s, bounty repeals, state game management, and the 1995 genetic rescue releasing eight Texas females boosted Florida panthers above 200 while western cougars recolonized the Midwest.
region: Western & Southeastern North America, Central & South America

cause: Most threatened African ape (~250–300 individuals split across ~11 rugged forest fragments on the Nigeria–Cameroon border), facing wire snaring, bushmeat hunting, and logging.

Smallest natural range of any crocodilian (~2,400–3,000 pure animals restricted to Cuba's Zapata Swamp and Isla de la Juventud), imperiled by illegal hunting and genetic hybridization with American crocodiles.

Reduced across Europe to fragmented lakes by wetland drainage and persecution, artificial floating nesting rafts at Lake Prespa and Lake Kerkini, strict marsh protection, and power-line markers doubled European colonies and supported IUCN downlisting to Near Threatened.
World's largest gazelle reduced to fewer than 300 wild individuals across scattered Sahelian pockets in Chad, Niger, and Mali due to uncontrolled hunting and livestock overgrazing.
Temperate Valdivian rainforest endemic (~600–1,000 individuals on Chiloé Island and coastal mainland Chile), threatened by logging, stray-dog attacks, and canine distemper.

Among the first animals listed under U.S. federal endangered species law in 1967 after logging shrunk its range by 90%, mature forest conservation easements on private farms and more than a dozen translocations grew numbers to ~20,000 and earned U.S. ESA delisting in 2015.
Largest wolf spider on Earth (~4,000 individuals confined to a single high valley on Deserta Grande), squeezed by invasive canary-grass choking out rock crevices and introduced mice.
Smallest geographic range of any vertebrate: ~175–260 iridescent fish inhabit a single geothermal limestone cavern shelf in Nevada, threatened by aquifer drawdown, warming water, and flash floods.
region: Devils Hole, Mojave Desert, Nevada, USA

cause: Asiatic wild dog reduced to ~950–2,200 mature individuals by wild-ungulate prey depletion, forest conversion, livestock-retaliation poisoning, and disease spillover from feral dogs.
Close relative of the mandrill confined to a small Cross-Sanaga-Bioko range (~3,000–4,000 remaining), imperiled by commercial bushmeat hunting with dogs and palm-oil deforestation.
Largest primate suffered >75% population collapse since the 1990s due to armed conflict, artisanal coltan and gold mining camps, and bushmeat poaching in eastern DRC.
region: Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo

cause: Shrunk to fewer than 100,000 North American elk by 1900 after Eastern and Merriam’s subspecies were driven extinct, winter refuge protection, Yellowstone herd transplants across 40+ states, and habitat partnerships rebuilt North American numbers past 1 million.
Primary shallow wave-breaking coral of Caribbean reefs decimated >90% by white-band and white-pox diseases, acute thermal bleaching events, acidification, and coastal runoff.
region: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico & Florida Keys

cause: Afroalpine rodent-hunting specialist (~450–500 adults in Bale and Simien mountain enclaves), periodically devastated by rabies and canine distemper transmitted from village dogs.

Hunted nearly to extinction for fur and castoreum until roughly 1,200 animals survived in eight isolated refugia around 1900, legal hunting bans and dozens of European reintroductions—including Scotland and England—rebuilt the continental population past 1.5 million.

Exterminated across much of Central and Western Europe by bounty hunting and electrocution, strict European Union Birds Directive protections, power-pole retrofits, and captive-release projects enabled widespread natural recolonization.

Eradicated from nearly all of Western and Central Europe by the mid-20th century through fur trapping and bounty hunting, legal protections and Carpathian translocations since the 1970s re-established wild populations in the Alps, Jura, Vosges, and Dinaric mountains.

Nearly vanished across England, lowland Europe, and Japan from organochlorine pesticide bioaccumulation and river canalization in the 1950s–1970s, bans on dieldrin and PCBs coupled with cleaner rivers and riverbank corridors allowed otters to return to every English county.

Collapsed to roughly 300 Western European breeding pairs by the 1960s due to wetland drainage and chemical pollution, European wetland protection and flyway sanctuary networks tripled Western European colonies and spurred natural recolonization of Britain and Denmark.

Extinct in the wild by 1927 when just 54 individuals remained in zoos, an international pedigree-breeding effort launched from 12 founder lineages and wild releases starting in Białowieża Forest in 1952 rebuilt free-ranging herds past 7,000 and earned IUCN downlisting to Near Threatened in 2020.
Glass-eel recruitment crashed >90% since the 1980s from illicit trafficking of juvenile eels to East Asia, river hydropower turbines, invasive swim-bladder parasites, and shifting Atlantic currents.

Reduced in England to fewer than 100 individuals at a single West Sussex meadow by the late 1980s from heathland neglect, targeted pine-scrub clearing, sandy turf management, and multi-year zoo-bred translocations under "Back from the Brink" established multiple thriving UK colonies.
region: Western & Central Europe (UK Recovery in Southern England)

cause: Lost across >85% of its historic European riverine range due to competitive displacement by invasive American mink, wetland drainage, historical fur trapping, and road mortality.
region: Northern Spain, France, Danube Delta & Russia

cause: Presumed extinct for 50 years until rediscovered in 1989, landowner partnerships, controlled burns, and Kincaid’s lupine prairie restoration grew Oregon counts from ~3,000 to over 13,000 butterflies and led the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to downlist it from Endangered to Threatened in 2023.
Dry-forest arboreal iguana whose primary stronghold on Yadua Taba holds most of the remaining population, threatened elsewhere by feral goats, cats, rats, and invasive green iguanas.
region: Yadua Taba & Dry Western Islands, Fiji

cause: Slaughtered by the hundreds of thousands during 20th-century factory-ship whaling, the 1986 International Whaling Commission global commercial moratoria enabled slow but measurable oceanic recovery, roughly doubling global estimates past 100,000 and earning IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2018.

Wiped out across most of the northeastern and Great Lakes U.S. by 1930 from over-trapping and clear-cutting, trapping moratoria, forest regeneration, and interstate reintroductions across New England, the Upper Midwest, and Washington’s Cascades restored healthy populations.
region: Northern United States & Canadian Boreal Forests

cause: Fish-eating wetland specialist whose peat-swamp and riverine habitats across Sundaland are among the fastest-cleared ecosystems on Earth due to oil palm drainage and river pollution.
Island-endemic raptor (<100–250 mature individuals across Flores, Sumbawa, and Lombok), severely threatened by lowland forest clearing, livestock-predation persecution, and illegal pet capture.

Pushed to Critically Endangered when accidentally introduced brown rats invaded Frégate Island in 1995, an emergency Zoological Society of London captive-breeding program alongside island-wide rat eradication and woodland restoration rebuilt numbers and earned IUCN downlisting to Vulnerable in 2014.
Only equatorial penguin (~1,200 mature individuals) suffers catastrophic starvation crashes during intense El Niño marine heatwaves that shut down cold Humboldt/Cromwell nutrient upwellings.
Described only in 2009 and restricted exclusively to Wolf Volcano's upper slopes (~210–300 adults), facing catastrophic risk from volcanic eruptions, drought, and feral cat predation on hatchlings.
Vulnerable to intense El Niño ocean-warming events that collapse sardine prey stocks, alongside disease transmission from introduced dogs and plastic entanglement.
Blind echolocating river dolphin fragmented by more than 50 irrigation barrages and dams across South Asia, alongside gillnet entanglement, boat strikes, and heavy pollution.
Elusive true river shark reduced to tiny, rarely recorded numbers across Indian and Bangladeshi rivers by artisanal gillnets, dam barriers, and sand mining.
Narrow-snouted fish-eating crocodilian reduced to <800–900 breeding adults mostly along India's Chambal River by sand mining, irrigation dams, egg collection, and gillnet drowning.
region: Chambal & Ganges River Tributaries, India & Nepal

cause: World's largest bivalve (up to 1.4 m) uplisted to Critically Endangered in 2024 after losing >84% of wild populations over three generations to meat/shell harvesting and warming-induced bleaching.
Targeted across tropical fisheries for its gill plates sold in Asian traditional medicine markets, compounded by low fecundity (single pup every 2–5 years) and net bycatch.
Two-meter Amazonian apex river predator recovering unevenly from mid-20th-century pelt hunting, now threatened by artisanal gold-mining mercury contamination, deforestation, and overfishing.
region: Amazon, Orinoco & Pantanal Basins, South America

cause: Strict bamboo-forest reserves, anti-poaching enforcement, and corridor reforestation boosted wild numbers past 1,800, downlisting it from Endangered to Vulnerable.
World's largest scaly anteater has surged in illicit scale-trafficking volume as Asian pangolins grew scarce, compounded by bushmeat hunting and equatorial rainforest clearance.
Australia's rarest marsupial (~100–120 individuals after a 2015 wildfire burned 90% of Two Peoples Bay habitat), kept alive by feral cat/fox exclusion on island and mainland sanctuaries.
region: Two Peoples Bay & Bald Island, Western Australia

cause: Saved from ~200 individuals to several thousand in Brazil's coastal Atlantic Forest, yet remains Endangered due to severe habitat fragmentation, highway barriers, and yellow fever outbreaks.
region: Rio de Janeiro Atlantic Forest, Brazil

cause: Brilliantly colored poison-frog analog restricted to fragmented pandanus swamps around Moramanga, Madagascar, squeezed by slash-and-burn clearing, peat fires, nickel mining, and pet collection.
High-altitude temperate forest specialist fragmented into isolated mountain subpopulations across central China by historical logging, highway corridors, and tourism pressure.
Iridescent cobalt-blue arboreal tarantula restricted to <100 km² of degraded deciduous forest in Andhra Pradesh, threatened by firewood logging, civil infrastructure, and live exotic-pet smuggling.

Formerly Endangered when breeding pairs fell below 250 on Cabbage Tree Island due to invasive rabbits and sticky bird-lime tree tangles, rabbit eradication, avian predator control, and chick translocations to Boondelbah Island drove its downlisting to Vulnerable in 2004.

Devastated by commercial shore and lagoon whaling until barely 2,000 Eastern North Pacific whales remained in the 1930s, International Whaling Commission protections and Mexican breeding-lagoon sanctuaries drove recovery past 20,000 and U.S. Endangered Species Act delisting in 1994.
region: North Pacific Ocean (Baja California to Chukchi Sea)

cause: Exterminated across the contiguous western U.S. and much of Western Europe by predator-control bounties, Endangered Species Act reintroductions in Yellowstone and Idaho (1995–1996) alongside European Habitats Directive protections spurred widespread natural recolonization.
Uplisted to Critically Endangered (<1,000 mature birds) after selective logging of towering Dipteryx almendro nesting trees and intensive chick capture for the illegal cage-bird trade.
Suffers extreme post-release capture mortality and heavy fishing pressure for the international shark-fin trade, driving global declines exceeding 80% over three generations.
Heaviest flying grassland bird (<150 individuals left mostly in Rajasthan's Thar Desert), devastated by conversion of arid steppes and fatal collisions with high-voltage solar and wind powerlines.

Once numbering barely 1,200 birds globally due to wetland loss and nesting-tree felling, grassroots village stewardship led by Assam’s "Hargila Army" safeguarded nesting groves and rescued fallen chicks, helping grow global estimates above 3,000 and earning IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Near Threatened in 2023.

After decades of nesting-beach patrols, egg-harvest bans, Turtle Excluder Devices on shrimp trawlers, and international trade treaties, global nesting populations rebounded across major rookeries from Ascension Island to Tortuguero, driving an October 2025 IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Least Concern.
Largest wild equid (~2,800 individuals left in northern Kenya and Ethiopia), compressed by pastoralist waterhole exclusion, climate-intensified Horn of Africa droughts, and habitat loss.

Captive breeding, protected cliff sanctuaries, supplementary carcass feeding sites, and flagship reintroduction programs in France’s Grands Causses and the Alps reversed 20th-century declines and expanded breeding numbers across Iberia and the Balkans.
region: Southern Europe, North Africa & Southwest Asia

cause: Presumed extinct twice after 19th-century commercial sealers slaughtered colonies for pelts, Mexican island-reserve protection in 1922 and the U.S. Marine Mammal Protection Act enabled steady growth from a handful of survivors past 30,000 individuals and IUCN downlisting to Least Concern.

Previously depleted by up to 90% from sheep-ranching competition and commercial pelt hunting, CITES Appendix II export regulations, large Patagonian national parks, and provincial sustainable-use rules restored over 1.5 million wild guanacos.
World's rarest primate with only ~37–42 individuals left in a single forest patch at Bawangling on Hainan Island, critically vulnerable to genetic bottlenecks and typhoons.

Confined to a tiny rocky boulder bank on Stephens Island and threatened by habitat loss and predators, biosecurity protection, tuatara exclusion fencing, and conservation translocations to Maud Island and sanctuaries supported IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2017.
region: Takapourewa (Stephens) & Te Pākeka (Maud) Islands, New Zealand

cause: Slashed >80% over three generations by centuries of tortoiseshell (bekko) harvesting, egg collection, coral-reef bleaching degradation, and coastal gillnet and longline bycatch.
Coastal New Zealand endemic severely impacted by set-net and trawl bycatch, toxoplasmosis runoff, and coastal vessel disturbance; its Māui subspecies numbers fewer than 60.
Uplisted from Near Threatened straight to Critically Endangered due to explosive poaching for its solid keratin casque ('red ivory') carved for black-market ornaments, plus old-growth logging.
Sole living member of its genus (~300–500 animals along the Kenya–Somalia border), declining after rinderpest, poaching, elephant loss causing shrub encroachment, and severe droughts.
Largest butterfly in the Americas, restricted to just two tiny remnant montane rainforest pockets in Jamaica where coffee farming, timber logging, and illegal specimen collecting erode survival.
Living fossil amphibian presumed extinct for 56 years after the 1950s drainage of Israel's Hula Marshes until its dramatic 2011 rediscovery; fewer than a few hundred remain in tiny restored springs.
After industrial whaling killed ~90% of populations, the 1982 IWC commercial whaling moratorium allowed global numbers to rebound to ~80,000+.
Two-meter coral-reef giant heavily depleted across the Coral Triangle by live-reef luxury restaurant fishing, destructive cyanide capture, spear-fishing, and coral-bleaching habitat loss.

Threatened by the illegal wild-bird trade and habitat clearing, CITES Appendix I trade bans, artificial nest boxes, and rancher partnerships spearheaded by the Hyacinth Macaw Project stabilized Pantanal strongholds and enabled IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2014.
Saved from under 100 individuals in 2002 to over 2,000 today via captive breeding, rabbit prey restoration, and highway wildlife corridors; downlisted to Vulnerable in 2024.
Strict shallow-coast specialist suffering high mortality from artisanal gillnets, port dredging, coastal reclamation, and chemical pollution across the Indian Ocean rim.

Reduced to fewer than 200 individuals around 1900 by sport hunting and horn poaching, strict armed protection in Kaziranga and Chitwan national parks alongside floodplain translocations rebuilt over 4,000 rhinos and earned IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2008.
region: Assam, West Bengal & Terai Arc (India & Nepal)

cause: Cliff-nesting scavenger wiped out by >97% across India and Pakistan due to lethal veterinary NSAIDs (diclofenac and aceclofenac) persisting in cattle carcasses despite regulatory bans.
Largest living lemur fails to survive in captivity and depends strictly on intact eastern Malagasy rainforest, which is rapidly vanishing to slash-and-burn agriculture and bushmeat hunting.
Confined to isolated stretches between massive Indus River irrigation barrages (~1,800 individuals), vulnerable to dry-season water diversion, canal stranding, and net bycatch.
Estuarine and riverine populations face catastrophic gillnet bycatch, electrofishing, hydropower damming, and gold-mining mercury pollution; Mekong subpopulations hold <100 animals.
region: South & Southeast Asian Coasts and Rivers

cause: Crashed by over 95% on several Channel Islands around 2000 due to hyperpredation by invasive golden eagles sustained on feral pigs, rapid captive breeding, pig eradication, and golden eagle relocation produced the fastest mammal recovery delisting in U.S. Endangered Species Act history in 2016.

Listed as U.S. Threatened in 1977 after feral goats, pigs, and rabbits devastated native cactus and boxthorn scrub, U.S. Navy and National Park Service herbivore eradications restored vegetation and allowed populations to surpass 20 million, earning ESA delisting in 2014.
region: San Clemente, San Nicolas & Santa Barbara Islands, California

cause: Restricted to a single population in Ujung Kulon National Park (~70 individuals), imperiled by poaching, invasive Arenga palms, and tsunami/volcanic risk.

Thought extinct until a small breeding colony of roughly 200 seals was rediscovered in 1965 after millions were killed in the 18th–19th century fur trade, strict Chilean National Park protection and total sealing bans rebuilt the population past 30,000.
Flightless, crested evolutionary relict endemic to New Caledonia (~1,000–2,000 birds), heavily preyed upon by feral dogs, pigs, cats, and rats while nickel mining fragments cloud forests.
Flightless nocturnal parrot decimated by introduced mammalian predators; ~240 individuals survive exclusively on predator-free offshore sanctuaries.
World's smallest and most endangered sea turtle; relies primarily on a single Gulf beach (Rancho Nuevo), making it vulnerable to shrimp-trawl bycatch, oil spills, and coastal warming.
region: Gulf of Mexico & Western North Atlantic

cause: Falling to 167 singing males in 1974 and 1987 due to wildfire suppression and brown-headed cowbird brood parasitism, prescribed jack-pine burns and cowbird trapping multiplied singing males above 2,300 and earned U.S. Endangered Species Act delisting in 2019.

World's largest living lizard (~1,380 mature adults across Komodo, Rinca, Flores, and Gili Motang), uplisted to Endangered in 2021 due to rising sea levels shrinking lowland habitat and deer prey loss.

Declining to roughly 1,500 adults by 1999 due to shoreline armoring and intentional killing, public outreach campaigns ("Respect the Snake") alongside rocky shoreline easements tripled adult abundance past 10,000 and earned U.S. ESA delisting in 2011.
Fully aquatic skin-breathing giant frog endemic to high-altitude Lake Titicaca, hit hard by untreated municipal and mining pollution, chytrid outbreaks, introduced trout, and tonic-drink harvesting.

Declared extinct in Britain in 1979 after agricultural change erased the warm short-turf grasslands needed by its host Myrmica sabuleti ants, ecological research by Jeremy Thomas restored grazed chalk hills and successfully reintroduced Swedish stock across dozens of UK reserves.
Giant euryhaline ray lost from most tropical rivers and coasts due to gillnet entanglement, targeted fin and rostrum trade, and freshwater dam construction.
Victoria's arboreal 'fairy possum' lost vital old-growth hollow-bearing mountain ash trees to the 2009 Black Saturday megafires and decades of clearfell forestry.
Cliff-nesting Caatinga parrot (~1,700–2,200 individuals after decades of protection), still pressured by licuri palm-nut habitat degradation from goat grazing and illegal chick poaching.
Nocturnal Central American treefrog wiped from >80% of its historic Costa Rican and Panamanian cloud-forest sites by chytridiomycosis epidemics and tropical forest loss.

Previously listed as Vulnerable due to steppe habitat loss and pesticides, pan-European LIFE projects installing thousands of artificial nest cavities on historic buildings and restoring dry grassland foraging stabilized numbers and earned downlisting to Least Concern.
region: Mediterranean Basin, Eastern Europe & Central Asia

cause: Listed as U.S. Endangered in 1988 with fewer than 1,000 known individuals in 14 roosts, binational cave-roost gating, public education, and bat-friendly agave harvesting partnerships across Mexico and Arizona lifted numbers past 200,000 and secured the first-ever bat delisting under the U.S. ESA in 2018.
Declared extinct in 1920 after shipwrecked black rats overran Lord Howe Island until ~24 wild 'tree lobsters' were rediscovered in 2001 clinging to a single shrub on sea stack Ball's Pyramid.
region: Ball's Pyramid (off Lord Howe Island), Australia

cause: Among the rarest raptors on Earth (~120 breeding pairs along northwestern Madagascar coasts and wetlands), squeezed by lake siltation, overfishing, mangrove felling, and human persecution.
World's rarest duck, feared extinct until 22 individuals were rediscovered at Lake Matsaborimena in 2006; marsh drainage, siltation, and exotic fish still limit wild recovery.
Only Old World tapir (~2,500 individuals remaining), suffering rapid rainforest conversion for palm oil and rubber plantations, reservoir flooding, and increasing highway collisions.
Plunged below 150 individuals in Peninsular Malaysia due to commercial wire-snare poaching syndicates, canine distemper outbreaks, and rainforest fragmentation for highways and agriculture.

Once Endangered by poaching, military conflict, and grazing competition, community-managed mountain conservancies in Pakistan and Tajikistan that channel conservation-permit revenue back into local villages halted poaching and lifted numbers past 5,700 mature adults, earning IUCN downlisting to Near Threatened in 2015.
region: Mountains of Pakistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan & India

cause: Once considered the rarest parrot in the world with barely 12 known birds in the 1980s, intensive nest guarding, chick rescuing, invasive predator control, and supplementary feeding rebuilt wild numbers past 700 birds and drove IUCN downlistings from Critically Endangered to Vulnerable in 2019.

Three-meter, 300-kg freshwater behemoth declined by >80–90% in recent decades due to historical overfishing, channel blasting, sand dredging, and mainstream Mekong hydropower dams blocking spawning migrations.

Listed as Endangered in 1985 due to stream incision, grazing erosion, and hybridization, collaborative riparian fencing, culvert passage fixes, and non-native trout removal with local ranchers tripled stream occupancy and secured U.S. ESA delisting in 2016.
region: Pit River Watershed, Northeastern California & Oregon

cause: Europe's most threatened amphibian (~1,000–1,500 individuals confined to fewer than 8 km² of cold beech-forest streams on Catalonia's Montseny Massif), imperiled by warming droughts and water extraction.

Once Endangered after commercial hide hunting reduced wild numbers in Mexico and Central America, strict Mexican hunting bans (1970), CITES regulation, and trinational monitoring rebuilt wild populations and earned U.S. Endangered Species Act delisting in 2012.
Giant Caribbean whistling frog lost >99% of its wild numbers in Dominica and Montserrat after volcanic eruptions, overharvesting, and a devastating chytrid fungal epidemic.
Rebounded past 1,000 individuals through veterinary patrols and ecotourism, yet remains Endangered due to habitat compression and human-borne disease.

Australia's only hibernating alpine mammal (<2,000 individuals across boulderfields above 1,300 m), threatened by declining winter snowpack insulation, ski-resort development, and Bogong moth collapses.

Once IUCN Critically Endangered (1996) after river regulation, irrigation pumps, and heavy fishing collapsed stocks, fishways across weirs, strict slot catch limits, and restocking stabilized wild recruitment enough for IUCN reassessment down to Least Concern in 2019 (while remaining Vulnerable under Australian national law).

Extirpated from Alaska in the 19th century and nearly wiped out in Arctic Canada by fur and meat hunting, strict Canadian hunting moratoria (1917) and translocations of Greenland muskoxen to Nunivak Island, Alaska, Norway, and Siberia rebuilt circumpolar numbers past 130,000.
Large Caribbean reef predator whose predictable winter full-moon spawning aggregations were systematically targeted and wiped out across most reefs, cutting populations >80%.

Lost from over 70% of British inland heathland sites during the 20th century due to pool acidification and conifer planting, dune-slack scraping, livestock grazing, and head-starting translocations have restored self-sustaining British and Irish breeding colonies.

Reduced to roughly 30 birds in 1952 by hunting, habitat loss, and introduced mongooses, decades of captive breeding by Peter Scott and Hawaiian biologists plus predator control at national parks restored more than 3,000 wild birds and earned US ESA downlisting to Threatened in 2019.

Widely depleted between the 1940s and 1960s by commercial leather harvesting, international CITES trade quotas, regulated ranching programs, and national park wetland protections across southern and eastern Africa restored healthy wild populations.
Mediterranean's largest endemic bivalve (up to 1.2 m) suffered near-100% mass mortality since 2016 from an invasive Haplosporidium pinnae parasite spreading across warming seagrass meadows.

Previously restricted in Britain to clean water-soldier ditches in the Norfolk and Suffolk Broads due to marsh drainage and eutrophication, improved agricultural water quality, ditch restoration, and wetland conservation drove rapid British range expansion into Kent, Essex, and Wales.
region: Eastern & Southern England and Continental Europe

cause: Reduced to an estimated 100,000 survivors by 1900 after centuries of industrial fur trapping, strict state trapping limits, watershed protections, and backcountry restocking (including famous 1948 parachute drops in Idaho) restored tens of millions across North American rivers.

Extirpated across large portions of the U.S. Midwest and Appalachia by 1900 due to unregulated fur trapping and industrial water pollution, Clean Water Act watershed improvements and 20+ state reintroduction programs translocating over 4,000 otters restored nationwide populations.
Fewer than 370 individuals remain due to lethal vessel strikes in busy shipping lanes, commercial fishing-gear entanglements, and climate-driven prey shifts.

Reduced to fewer than 330 pairs in the 1990s by introduced possums and ship rats, sustained landscape-scale predator trapping, fenced sanctuaries, and community translocations lifted populations above 2,000 pairs and improved global status to Least Concern.
region: North Island Mainland Sanctuaries, New Zealand

cause: Never recovered from 19th–20th-century industrial and illegal Soviet whaling; only a few hundred individuals survive amid ship traffic, entanglement, and warming Bering Sea prey shifts.
Extirpated across Europe and Syria; ~700–800 wild birds survive along Morocco's Souss-Massa coast (plus reintroduced European flocks), facing coastal resort expansion and pesticide risk.

Hunted for blubber oil until fewer than 100 individuals survived on Mexico’s Guadalupe Island in the 1890s, strict Mexican and U.S. marine-mammal protections allowed the species to surge past 200,000 animals and recolonize mainland California rookeries such as Año Nuevo and Piedras Blancas.
region: Pacific Coast of Mexico, California & Oregon

cause: One of the rarest large land mammals (~315–400 individuals in two fenced Queensland reserves), pushed to the edge by historical sheep grazing, drought, invasive buffel grass, and wild dogs.
region: Epping Forest & Richard Underwood Reserves, Queensland, Australia

cause: Wiped out across 99% of its range by introduced red foxes and feral cats until only two Western Australian remnants survived, broad-scale fox baiting ("Western Shield"), Perth Zoo breeding, and fenced-sanctuary translocations lifted populations past 2,000 and earned IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Near Threatened.
Once one of the most abundant pelagic sharks, collapsed by >98% in parts of its range due to tuna longline bycatch and relentless demand for its paddle-like fins.

Endangered since 1973 after road erosion and impoundments degraded sandy Panhandle creeks, over 25 years of culvert replacements, borrow-pit restoration, and stream stabilization with Eglin Air Force Base expanded numbers above 600,000 and achieved U.S. ESA delisting in 2023.
Only living relative of the giraffe, endemic to northeastern DRC rainforests, halved in two decades by armed militia presence, illegal gold mining, logging, and bushmeat snaring.

Depleted by mass commercial slaughter at nesting beaches and fishery bycatch, Mexico’s 1990 total sea-turtle ban, community beach protection in Costa Rica and India, and TEDs on fishing fleets helped arribada nesting numbers surge and earned IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2008.
One of the world's rarest migratory birds (~70–80 wild individuals arriving at Melaleuca, Tasmania), imperiled by coastal saltmarsh loss on mainland wintering grounds and beak-and-feather disease.

Listed as U.S. Endangered in 1993 with fewer than 1,000 fish surviving in eight sloughs after dam flood-control and invasive bass predation, floodplain reconnection and Safe Harbor landowner ponds multiplied numbers past 140,000 across ~80 sites, making it the first fish delisted under the U.S. ESA in 2015.
One of the largest reptiles in the Americas, never recovered from mid-20th-century commercial hide slaughter (<250–1,000 wild adults left), facing egg collection, river pollution, and habitat loss.

Following severe mid-20th-century crashes caused by DDT-induced eggshell thinning, national DDT bans, artificial nesting platforms, and regional reintroduction programs restored thriving breeding populations across North America and Europe.

Iconic cloud-forest harlequin toad decimated across western Panama by lethal chytridiomycosis (Bd fungus) and stream loss; rated Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) while surviving in captive assurance colonies.
region: El Valle de Antón & Western Highlands, Panama

cause: World's most endangered crocodile (~90–140 mature wild individuals in northern Luzon and Mindanao marshes), threatened by dynamite fishing, wetland conversion to rice paddies, and persecution.
Massive monkey-eating forest raptor (~400 pairs left mainly on Mindanao and Luzon), severely constrained by dipterocarp deforestation, mining, and accidental trapping or shooting.

Reduced to roughly 10 wild individuals in 1990 by cyclone damage, deforestation, and invasive predators, decades of captive breeding by the Durrell Trust and Mauritian Wildlife Foundation alongside forest restoration lifted numbers above 400 and achieved IUCN downlisting to Vulnerable in 2018.
World's rarest tortoise (<400 wild individuals around Baly Bay, Madagascar), pushed toward biological extinction in the wild by ruthless luxury pet-trade poaching and bushfires.

Declared extinct in Britain by 1995 after pingo pond drainage and habitat shading wiped out its last Norfolk site, genetic research identifying Swedish frogs as the same native northern clade led to pond restoration and successful reintroductions starting in 2005.
region: Northern & Central Europe (Reintroduced to Norfolk, UK)

cause: Bornean riverine and mangrove forest clearing for shrimp aquaculture, oil palm plantations, and coastal settlements has split populations and opened them to hunting.

Cut from tens of millions to around 13,000 individuals by 1915 through market hunting and barbed-wire fencing, interstate wildlife sanctuaries, wildlife-friendly fence retrofits, and regulated hunting restored roughly 1 million pronghorns across western sagebrush steppes.
Declared Extinct in the Wild in 1969; international zoo breeding reintroduced self-sustaining herds back onto the Mongolian and Kazakh steppes.
Secretive West African rainforest hippo (<2,500 mature individuals), losing swamp habitats to commercial logging, mining, and rice farming while exposed to bushmeat hunting.
region: Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea & Côte d'Ivoire

cause: World's smallest suid (<400 wild individuals surviving in Assam's Manas and reintroduction sites), threatened by alluvial grassland burning, flood-control grazing, and agricultural encroachment.
Endemic solely to tiny Isla Escudo de Veraguas off Panama (<100–300 individuals), squeezed by mangrove timber cutting, tourism encroachment, and extreme genetic isolation.
World's largest butterfly (wingspan up to 28 cm), confined to fragmented Oro Province lowland rainforest in Papua New Guinea after the 1951 Mount Lamington eruption and oil palm clearing.
Ornate star-patterned Malagasy tortoise stripped from southern spiny forests by tens of thousands annually for illegal international pet trafficking and local bushmeat consumption.

Standing at only 29 birds in 1989 and once ranked among the world’s rarest songbirds, intensive seasonal rat poisoning in the Takitumu Conservation Area plus an insurance translocation to Ātiu boosted numbers above 500 and enabled downlisting to Vulnerable in 2018.

Seafloor-walking anglerfish restricted to two tiny rocky reef patches in southeastern Tasmania (<100 adults left), imperiled by urchin barrens destroying spawning seaweed, warming seas, and coastal runoff.

Reduced in Britain to a tiny Welsh remnant by historical poisoning and persecution, coordinated translocation programs from Spain and Sweden starting in 1989 coupled with bans on illegal poison baits sparked rapid recovery across Great Britain and Europe.
World's most endangered canid (~15–20 wild individuals in eastern North Carolina), hammered by illegal gunshot killings, vehicle strikes, and hybridization with expanding coyotes.

Decimated by the loss of open mature pine savannas, decades of prescribed fire management, artificial nest-cavity inserts, and Safe Harbor landowner agreements tripled active territories to nearly 7,800 groups and led to U.S. ESA downlisting from Endangered to Threatened in 2024.
region: Southeastern United States Longleaf Pine Forests

cause: Uplisted to Critically Endangered as widespread snaring, poaching for traditional medicine, and forest fragmentation across Vietnam and Laos slash wild numbers.
Dwindled to ~250–300 wild birds in southeastern Australia due to box-ironbark woodland clearing and intense bushfires; so scarce that wild males are losing their cultural courtship song.
Newly described baleen whale restricted to ~50 individuals in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico, imperiled by offshore oil spills, seismic survey noise, and vessel collisions.
Despite familiarity in zoos, wild populations plunged due to destruction of southern Madagascar gallery and spiny forests for charcoal, plus illegal domestic pet capture.

Pushed down to just 5–6 surviving pairs in the late 1960s by deforestation and cyclones, large-scale native woodland replanting on Rodrigues allowed the endemic songbird to surge into the tens of thousands and achieve IUCN downlisting to Least Concern in 2025.

Nearly wiped out when native forest cover shrank to fragmented gullies in the 1970s, community-led watershed reforestation and invasive tree management restored woodland habitat across Rodrigues and supported IUCN downlisting to Least Concern in 2025.
Driven nearly to extinction across Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana by relentless bushmeat hunting and clearance of Upper Guinean canopy forests for cocoa farming.

Reduced to roughly 30 breeding pairs in Florida during the 1930s after the plume trade and disturbance decimated rookeries, federal bird-protection laws and mangrove sanctuary enforcement enabled steady recovery and northward range expansion along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
region: Gulf Coast, Florida, Caribbean & South America

cause: Cut down to roughly 50–75 snakes in the 1970s after introduced rabbits and goats stripped Round Island bare, eradication of invasive herbivores, native palm forest regeneration, and translocation to Gunner’s Quoin lifted numbers past 1,000 and secured IUCN downlisting to Vulnerable in 2018.
Once abundant across 28 US states and two Canadian provinces before losing ~87% of its range since the late 1990s due to pathogen spillover from commercial bees, neonicotinoids, and prairie loss.

Collapsed by over 95% after the Soviet breakup and devastated again by a 2015 mass-mortality event, coordinated anti-poaching enforcement, expanded protected steppes, and international horn-trade controls drove Kazakhstan herds past 1.9 million and prompted a historic IUCN downlisting from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened in 2023.

Reduced to roughly 3,000 wild individuals in northern Australia by 1971 after decades of commercial skin hunting, federal export bans, state hunting prohibitions, and sustainable ranching partnerships rebuilt Australian populations past 100,000 and secured IUCN Least Concern status.
region: Northern Australia, Southeast Asia & Eastern India

cause: Eliminated across most of the American Midwest by the 1930s due to unregulated shooting and marsh drainage, federal protection under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act alongside prairie-wetland restoration rebuilt North American numbers to more than 800,000 birds.
Elusive Annamite Mountain forest bovid pushed to the brink by indiscriminate wire-snare trapping and logging fragmentation.
Aggregating schooling behavior makes it intensely vulnerable to industrial purse-seine and longline fleets targeting its large, high-value dorsal and pectoral fins.
Keystone kelp-forest predator reduced to tiny fragments during the maritime fur trade; lingering vulnerabilities include oil spills, killer-whale predation, shark bites, and infectious pathogens.

Iconic long-legged snake-hunting raptor uplisted to Endangered in 2020 after rapid savanna declines driven by agricultural expansion, frequent bushfires, powerline collisions, and pesticide poisoning.
Depleted by intensive 20th-century pelagic whaling, modern populations remain threatened by shipping collisions, fishing entanglement, and climate-induced zooplankton changes.

Confined to a single degraded mangrove patch of only 26 birds on Cousin Island in 1959, native Pisonia forest restoration and conservation translocations to five predator-free islands rebuilt over 3,000 birds and earned downlisting to Near Threatened.

Once believed nearly extinct with fewer than 50 individuals remaining on Mahé, successful translocations to rat-free North, Frégate, and Cousine islands established thriving satellite populations and prompted IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016.

Thought extinct in the 1940s after feather hunters killed millions, rediscovery of roughly 10 pairs on volcanic Torishima led Japanese biologist Hiroshi Hasegawa and partners to stabilize nesting slopes, deploy decoys, and enforce fisheries bycatch rules, lifting the population past 7,000.
Fastest-swimming shark is heavily overfished for both meat and fins in pelagic longline and gillnet fisheries while reproducing too slowly to offset catch rates.
Extirpated from 99% of its Southeast Asian river range by skin hunting and wetland rice conversion; ~400–1,000 pure wild crocodiles persist mainly in Cambodia's Cardamom Mountains.
Highly aquatic crane whose western and central flyways nearly vanished; almost the entire remaining ~4,000–5,000 birds winter at Poyang Lake, threatened by Yangtze damming and wetland drainage.
Known as the 'ghost of the forest,' fewer than 250 mature individuals remain in Marojejy and Makira cloud forests due to illegal rosewood logging and bushmeat poaching.
Extirpated across >80% of its Atlantic range because its toothed rostrum snags easily in trawls and gillnets, compounded by coastal mangrove nursery destruction.

Famous for halting Tellico Dam at the U.S. Supreme Court in 1978, successful river translocations, dam-tailwater oxygen improvements, and discovery of additional populations led to U.S. ESA downlisting to Threatened in 1984 and complete delisting due to recovery in 2022.

Threatened by poaching, prey loss, and retaliatory killings over livestock, community-run predator-proof corrals, livestock-insurance schemes, and the 12-nation Global Snow Leopard Program reduced conflict and supported IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2017.
region: High Mountains of Central & South Asia

cause: Slaughtered nearly to extirpation across North America in the late 1800s for breeding plumes worn on women’s hats, early Audubon Society sanctuary wardens and the 1918 Migratory Bird Treaty Act halted plume harvesting and restored coastal and inland nesting rookeries.

When ship rats invaded Big South Cape Island in 1964, wildlife officers rescued 36 birds—the entire surviving species—and translocated them to rat-free islets, launching island-hopping restorations that rebounded numbers into the thousands.
Warm-blooded migratory tuna driven below 10% of pre-industrial spawning biomass by high-seas sashimi longlining and juvenile purse-seining; slow gradual recovery keeps it Endangered.
region: Southern Hemisphere Oceans & Java Spawning Grounds

cause: Striking black-and-yellow alpine sphagnum frog reduced to <50 wild individuals in Kosciuszko National Park by chytridiomycosis, feral horses trampling bogs, and catastrophic 2019–2020 bushfires.
region: Kosciuszko National Park, New South Wales, Australia

cause: Hunted down to roughly 300 survivors by early 20th-century commercial whaling, international whaling bans starting in 1935 and coastal nursery-bay protections off Península Valdés, South Africa, and southern Australia drove sustained recovery above 13,000 whales.

Rebounded from roughly 30 breeding pairs in the 1960s to hundreds of pairs across Spain and Portugal after banning toxic predator baits, insulating lethal power lines, and protecting nesting estates under EU LIFE conservation programs.
