Spatulate-billed Arctic migrant reduced to <400 breeding pairs by intertidal mudflat reclamation along the Yellow Sea flyway and mist-net trapping on Southeast Asian wintering coasts.

Estuarine walking fish confined to Tasmania's Derwent Estuary (<2,000–3,000 individuals), devastated by invasive Northern Pacific seastars preying on stalked-ascidian egg substrates, dredging, and urban runoff.
Once-dominant Caribbean reef-builder collapsed >95% since the 1980s due to white-band disease, marine heatwave bleaching, ocean acidification, hurricane breakage, and nutrient pollution.
region: Caribbean Sea, Bahamas & Florida Reef Tract

cause: Following steep late-20th-century crashes driven by culling, fishery interactions, and nutritional stress, rookery exclusion zones, Marine Mammal Protection Act rules, and groundfish fishery protections drove sustained growth across the eastern stock, prompting U.S. ESA delisting of the eastern DPS in 2013.
region: North Pacific Rim (Japan, Alaska to California)

cause: Following severe spawning-stock collapse across Chesapeake Bay and the Hudson River in the late 1970s, the 1984 Atlantic Striped Bass Conservation Act enforced multi-state fishing moratoria and size limits that declared coastal stocks fully rebuilt by 1995.
region: Atlantic Coast & Chesapeake Bay, North America

cause: Rapid deforestation of Leuser peat-swamp forests for palm oil plantations, road expansion, and illegal pet trade.
Smallest and hairiest rhino (<50–80 individuals left) split into isolated pockets across Sumatra and Kalimantan, imperiled by horn poaching, tiny population Allee effects, and reproductive failure.
Last surviving Sunda island tiger (<400–600 individuals), cornered by rapid conversion of lowland forests into oil palm and pulpwood plantations and persistent bone-and-pelt poaching.
Most heavily trafficked wild mammal on Earth; hundreds of thousands have been seized from transnational wildlife smuggling rings supplying scale and luxury-meat markets.
Lost >90% of its global population (nearly 5.75 billion animals) after the 2013 sea-star wasting epidemic amplified by ocean warming, triggering urchin barrens and kelp-forest collapses.

Declared extirpated in Canada by 1938 and eradicated from roughly 90% of its historic grassland range by rodent-poisoning campaigns and plowing, coordinated captive-release reintroductions beginning in 1983 rebuilt self-sustaining populations across Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Montana.
Fastest migratory parrot (~500–750 wild birds left), collapsing from logging of Tasmanian blue-gum nesting forests and severe nest predation by introduced sugar gliders.

After intense pelagic longline fishing depleted North Atlantic swordfish biomass well below sustainable thresholds in the 1990s, ICCAT minimum-size rules, strict total allowable catch quotas, and nursery-area closures rebuilt the North Atlantic stock above management targets.
Flightless alpine swamphen rediscovered in 1948 after being presumed extinct; ~500 birds survive across Murchison Mountains and sanctuaries under strict stoat-trapping protection.
Dwarf wild buffalo endemic exclusively to Mindoro Island (~500–600 individuals), confined to grassy upland refuges by cattle ranching, snare poaching, and livestock diseases.

Driven extinct on mainland South Australia by introduced foxes, cooperative breeding and translocations—using heritage South Australian individuals accidentally preserved in New Zealand—alongside Western Shield predator control rebuilt mainland colonies and delisted it from Western Australia’s threatened fauna list.
Rarest great ape (<800 individuals in Batang Toru, Sumatra), severely fragmented by hydropower dam construction, gold mining, agricultural clearing, and human-wildlife conflict.
Largest extant carnivorous marsupial lost >80% of wild numbers since 1996 to contagious Devil Facial Tumour Disease (DFTD), compounded by roadkill and low genetic diversity.
World's largest freshwater invertebrate (up to 5 kg, living 40+ years), declining from illegal poaching, agricultural siltation, clearing of shaded riverbank snags, and stream warming.

Plummeted below 75,000 animals in the 1990s due to industrial poaching for shahtoosh wool, establishment of Hoh Xil and Changtang nature reserves, strict armed anti-poaching patrols, and CITES bans doubled wild herds above 200,000 and earned IUCN downlisting from Endangered to Near Threatened in 2016.
Great oceanic wanderer breeding almost solely on Gough Island, suffering massive chick mortality from invasive house mice eating chicks alive in nests alongside longline fishing bycatch.

Nearly wiped out across the lower 48 U.S. states by 1933 with fewer than 70 known birds outside Alaska due to feather-trade hunting, Red Rock Lakes National Wildlife Refuge protection and regional captive-reintroduction programs restored over 60,000 wild swans.

Wiped out from mainland New Zealand by invasive rats and habitat loss, complete rat eradications across offshore islets, incubation-temperature head-starting, and mainland predator-fenced sanctuary releases (such as Zealandia) boosted populations past 60,000.
region: Offshore Islands & Mainland Sanctuaries, New Zealand

cause: Critically endangered (<10 individuals remaining) due to fatal drowning as bycatch in illegal gillnets targeting totoaba fish swim bladders.

Reduced to roughly 6,000–10,000 animals in the 1960s by unregulated fleece hunting, the 1969 Vicuña Convention, CITES protections, and Indigenous community live-shearing programs ("chaccu") transformed poachers into stewards and rebuilt Andean herds past 350,000.

Listed as U.S. Endangered in 1967 with roughly 1,200 Florida animals documented in early counts, mandatory boat-speed zones, warm-water spring sanctuaries, and rescue rehabilitation raised Florida numbers past 6,000 and led to U.S. ESA downlisting to Threatened in 2017.
region: Florida, Gulf Coast, Caribbean & Northern South America

cause: Ancient lobe-finned 'living fossil' (~300–500 individuals in deep volcanic reef caves off Comoros, Tanzania, and South Africa), increasingly caught as accidental deep-set gillnet and oilfish-line bycatch.
region: Comoros Archipelago & East African Deep Reefs

cause: Reduced to a fraction of its historic range by land clearing and invasive red foxes, integrated fox-baiting programs in Western Australia and landmark reintroductions to South Australia’s Flinders Ranges stabilized wild populations and supported IUCN status improvement to Near Threatened.
Folivorous marsupial plunged >80% in a decade across southwestern Australian peppermint woodlands due to coastal urban sprawl, hotter droughts, wildfires, and introduced fox predation.

Eliminated from mainland New Zealand by introduced rats until surviving solely on Little Barrier Island, Auckland Zoo and Butterfly Creek captive breeding released over 11,000 insects across predator-free islands and sanctuaries, improving its national status from Nationally Endangered to Nationally Increasing.
region: Te Hauturu-o-Toi & Restored Hauraki Gulf Islands, New Zealand

cause: World's largest extant fish has halved in abundance over 75 years due to targeted fisheries, tuna-purse-seine bycatch, and fatal strikes from large commercial ships.
First marine invertebrate listed under the US Endangered Species Act; commercial overfishing cut densities >99% so surviving deep-reef adults are often too far apart for broadcast fertilization.

Extirpated in Sweden, Switzerland, and the Netherlands by the mid-20th century from wetland drainage and electrocution, wet-meadow conservation, power-line insulation, and European rewilding projects—including Britain’s Knepp Estate—drove global pairs above 300,000.

Once numbered in the tens of millions across South Asia before suffering a catastrophic >99% collapse in the 1990s–2000s from acute kidney failure caused by veterinary diclofenac in livestock carcasses.

Wiped out across much of Western Europe by persecution and organochlorine pesticides by the 1970s, strict legal protection, supplemental winter feeding, and multi-country reintroductions in Scotland, Ireland, and England have driven a continental comeback.
region: Northern & Central Europe to East Asia

cause: Tallest North American bird climbed back from ~15 wild birds in 1941 to ~830 total today, yet remains Endangered due to powerline collisions, coastal oil/water threats, and illegal shooting.
region: Wood Buffalo (Canada) to Aransas Coast (Texas, USA)

cause: Genetically distinct sister species to domestic Bactrian camels (~1,000–1,800 wild animals in Gobi and Lop Nur deserts), threatened by mining roads, wolf predation, and domestic hybridization.

Extirpated across most eastern and midwestern U.S. states by 1900 due to deforestation and unregulated market hunting, cannon-net capture-and-transfer programs funded by the Pittman-Robertson Act plus woodland regeneration restored roughly 6–7 million wild turkeys.

Eliminated from the contiguous U.S. and reduced to northern remnants in Scandinavia by early 20th-century poisoning and fur trapping, bans on indiscriminate strychnine baits, harvest limits, and wilderness protection enabled gradual natural recolonization across the northern Rockies and Scandinavia.
region: Scandinavia, Boreal Eurasia & Northwestern North America

cause: Pushed toward extinction by early 1900s market hunting and swamp-forest clearing, complete U.S.–Canadian hunting bans from 1918 to 1941 combined with citizen-built nest-box campaigns restored millions of breeding pairs across North American riparian woodlands.
Last remaining freshwater cetacean in the Yangtze (~1,200 individuals), squeezed by heavy barge traffic, river dredging, hydropower dams, and industrial runoff.
World's most imperiled turtle with only two confirmed living males left after the 2023 death of a wild female in Vietnam, following decades of hunting, river damming, and pollution.
Mainland South Island colonies have crashed sharply due to warming oceans, set-net drowning, avian diphtheria outbreaks, and predation by introduced stoats and ferrets.

Improved stock monitoring, regional harvest-control rules, and FAD management measures across Pacific and Atlantic tuna commissions slowed overfishing and supported the 2021 IUCN Red List reassessment downlisting the species from Near Threatened to Least Concern.
Coral-reef carpet shark heavily declined across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean due to inshore gillnetting, bottom trawling, finning, and reef blast fishing.
